title: Medical Words in Plain Language
summary: By the end, learners can use official words for kinds of care (primary care, family doctor, nurse practitioner, walk-in clinic, emergency), explain Health Canada terms such as prescription, dose, side effect, allergy, and interaction, list questions to ask a doctor or pharmacist, and choose trustworthy Canadian sources — without treating this course as medical advice.

lessons.title: Why health words matter
lessons.html:
Health information is easier to use when the words are clear. Health Canada and the Public Health Agency of Canada publish a series called It’s Your Health: more than 150 easy-to-understand articles to help people make informed decisions about health and safety. That series is a place to read official, plain-language articles. It is not a diagnosis of your own health.

This course teaches words you may hear at a clinic or see on a medicine label. It does not train you to work in a medical office, code a bill, or give care to someone else.

Health Canada’s page on using medications safely says prescription and non-prescription medications can help treat diseases and conditions, but taking them correctly is important. All medications carry some risk. The page uses the words side effects (also called adverse reactions) for unwanted effects that can happen even when a product is used correctly. Examples it gives include a mild rash or a severe allergic reaction.

If a provider uses a word you do not know, ask them to say it in everyday language. Write the word down. You can also call 811 in Alberta for nurse advice, or 911 in a medical emergency. Those numbers come from official Alberta pages, not from this course guessing what you should do.

Do not use random websites or social media posts as your only source. Lesson 5 points to official Canadian pages.

lessons.title: Words for kinds of care
lessons.html:
Official Alberta pages use several care words. Learning them helps you choose the right door — without this course choosing it for you.

Primary care is described by Primary Care Alberta as the first step for most health concerns. It includes family doctors, nurse practitioners, and other providers who help with everyday needs such as checkups, advice when you are sick or injured, prescriptions and refills, long-term conditions, mental health concerns, and referrals for specialists, tests, or other services.

Alberta Find a Provider says:

  • A family doctor provides ongoing, complete care for people of all ages, and supports specialist or hospital care when needed.
  • A nurse practitioner can assess, diagnose, treat illnesses, prescribe medications, and provide ongoing care.
  • Walk-in clinics provide non-emergency medical care without an appointment for minor illnesses, injuries, and general health.

Diagnose, on that official description, is part of what a nurse practitioner can do: figure out an illness so it can be treated. Treat means providing care for the illness. Prescribe means authorizing a medication. This course still cannot diagnose or treat you.

Alberta’s Know Your Options page says to call 911 for a medical emergency. If you are unsure where to go, call 811 for advice on your symptoms (what you feel or notice) and care options.

These words help you understand a poster or a receptionist. They do not replace a clinician.

lessons.title: Words on a medicine label
lessons.html:
Health Canada talks about both prescription medications (you get them with a prescriber’s order) and non-prescription medications (you can buy them without that order). Always use medication as directed by your doctor or pharmacist: when to take it, how often, and for how long. Always read the product label.

A dose is how much you take at one time. Health Canada says you should also know what to do if you miss a dose, and when you should stop a medication. Do not guess. Ask the pharmacist.

A side effect or adverse reaction is an unwanted effect. It can be mild or severe. Health Canada says to report a side effect to your healthcare professional, and you can also report it to Health Canada.

Tell your provider about allergies and sensitivities, your other health conditions, and all medications you take, including natural health products such as vitamins and herbal remedies. An interaction is when a medication does not mix safely with certain foods, drinks, vitamins, or other products. Health Canada gives grapefruit juice as one example of a drink to ask about.

Keep medicines in their original containers, out of the reach of children, and return expired medicine to a pharmacy or local disposal depot. If you think someone has taken too much, get emergency help — do not use this course as poison-control advice. MyHealth Alberta lists the Poison and Drug Information Service (PADIS) at 1-800-332-1414, and 911 for emergencies.

lessons.title: Questions to ask, and a simple medicine list
lessons.html:
Clear questions protect you. Health Canada’s “using medications safely” page says to talk with your doctor, pharmacist, or other healthcare professional about all aspects of your medication. Ask:

  • why you are being prescribed the medication
  • how it should work
  • whether you will need regular check-ups or tests
  • how to reduce the risk of side effects and interactions with food, drinks, vitamins, or herbal supplements
  • when you should expect to start feeling better
  • if and when you should go back to your doctor
  • what to do if you miss a dose

Ask your pharmacist for written information about the medications you take. Health Canada authorizes a Patient Medication Information section in a drug’s product monograph, written in plain language so it is easier to understand. A one-page pharmacy printout is not always the same as that authorized information, so ask if you want the official patient information.

Health Canada offers a medication chart to track:

  • the name (brand name and ingredients)
  • the dosage
  • the time you take it
  • the reason you take it
  • side effects you notice

Include prescription medicines, non-prescription medicines, and natural health products. Share the list with your doctor and pharmacist. Using the same pharmacy, Health Canada says, helps the pharmacist see possible harmful interactions.

Mention if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning a pregnancy, and mention trouble swallowing pills or remembering doses. This is so your provider can advise you — not so this course can.

lessons.title: Where to find trustworthy Canadian health information
lessons.html:
When you look up a health word, start with official Canadian pages:

  • Health Canada and It’s Your Health articles on Canada.ca, for easy-to-understand health and safety information
  • Alberta.ca pages such as Know Your Options, AHCIP, and health cards, for how care works in Alberta
  • Primary Care Alberta and Alberta Find a Provider, for what primary care, family doctors, nurse practitioners, and walk-in clinics are
  • MyHealth Alberta official phone-number lists, including 911 and 811

These sources will not replace a conversation with a clinician. They can help you prepare questions and check that a word means what you think it means.

Be careful with:

  • social media tips that do not name an official source
  • sites from another country that may describe different drugs, doses, or systems (this course does not use those as source pages)
  • anyone, including this course, who claims to diagnose you from a word list

If you feel unwell and do not know where to go, call 811. If it is a medical emergency, call 911. If you need AHCIP or a health card, go back to the Alberta health-care basics course and the live Alberta.ca pages.

Finishing this course does not make you a nurse, medical office assistant, or billing specialist. It helps you ask clearer questions.

keptBack.sourceDisclaimer: This course explains everyday health words using official Canadian government and Alberta health-system pages. It is not medical advice, not a diagnosis or treatment, not a clinical or medical-office (CMAA) credential, and not a billing course. It cannot tell you what is wrong with you or which medicine to take. If you are having a medical emergency, call 911. For health advice, Albertans can call Health Link 811.
keptBack.builderNotes:
- Official Canadian / Alberta sources only. Do not add MedlinePlus, WebMD, Mayo Clinic, or MyHealth Healthwise topic pages.
- Do not invent dictionary definitions that were not on a fetched page. “Diagnose / treat / prescribe” are used as Alberta Find a Provider uses them for nurse practitioners.
- Health Canada’s child-prescription questions page (2010) was opened but not used as a main learner source, so this course does not become a pediatric-medicine lesson.
- PADIS 1-800-332-1414 was verified on MyHealth Alberta’s numbers page this session; re-check before rebuilds.
- No Ed2Go medical-terminology word-association text and no US billing codes.
